section_summary: The section opens with correspondence about Soviet recruitment for fishing work in the Kurile Islands, Japanese seed oysters for the U.S. Pacific coast, and the possible use of Japanese cultured pearl stocks for reparations. It then contains a Foreign Economic Administration report recommending the elimination of Japan’s aluminum and magnesium production capacity. The final pages begin a separate guide to administering production programs during the occupation of Japan; that guide continues beyond page 74.

subfiles.title: Organization of Kurile State Fishing Trust
subfiles.from: O. Edmund Clubb, American Consul General, Vladivostok
subfiles.about: Forwards a Soviet advertisement recruiting workers for fishing combines in the Kuril Islands.
subfiles.summary: Clubb submits the advertisement as evidence of Soviet plans for the islands’ economy.

subfiles.title: Kurile Gosrybtrest recruitment advertisement
subfiles.about: Offers permanent and seasonal employment in the Kuril State Fishing Trust.
subfiles.summary: Lists wages, rations, travel assistance, leave and other benefits for workers hired in Vladivostok.

subfiles.title: Seed Oysters from Japan
subfiles.about: Records Hutchins’s effort to learn whether Japanese seed oysters could reach U.S. growers by April.
subfiles.summary: The National Canners Association feared a shortage for West Coast growers. Hutchins proposed seeking information directly from Fiedler; Flory objected to bypassing State Department channels.

subfiles.title: Japanese cultured pearls and possible reparations
subfiles.about: Proposes locating and selling accumulated Japanese cultured pearls as reparations.
subfiles.summary: Solomon recounts his earlier pearl-culture business, its collapse, and the growth of Japan’s pearl industry. He argues that wartime stocks could yield substantial reparations if carefully marketed and offers his expertise.

subfiles.title: Introduction of John I. Solomon to Maurice Holland
subfiles.about: Introduces Solomon to a National Research Council writer studying Japanese pearl culture.
subfiles.summary: Dunn describes Solomon as a pioneer of pearl culture and suggests that he meet Maurice Holland.

subfiles.title: Solomon’s reply concerning cultured pearls
subfiles.about: Describes trade opposition to cultured pearls and disputes claims about identifying them.
subfiles.summary: Solomon blames Kunz and French pearl dealers for a boycott of his business. He describes later disputes over Japanese pearls and says cultivated pearls could pass through Bombay into the trade as natural pearls.

subfiles.title: Notice of Hugh M. Smith’s death
subfiles.about: Informs Solomon that Hugh M. Smith died in 1941.

subfiles.title: Request for an introduction to the Commissioner of Fisheries
subfiles.about: Seeks an introduction while considering postwar pearl-culture operations.
subfiles.summary: Solomon proposes replacing Japanese dominance of pearl culture in British, Dutch, Australian and Philippine waters.

subfiles.title: Request for assistance with Japanese seed oysters
subfiles.about: Forwards oyster growers’ correspondence and requests State Department advice.
subfiles.summary: Savage asks about reopening contact with seed-oyster growers near Sendai Bay.

subfiles.title: Pacific Coast Oyster Growers Association request
subfiles.about: Requests help obtaining Japanese seed oysters and opposes Yamashita’s role in the trade.
subfiles.summary: Mathias cites poor recent oyster sets in Washington waters.

subfiles.title: Inquiry on resuming imports of Japanese seed oysters
subfiles.from: F. W. Mathias, Pacific Coast Oyster Growers Association
subfiles.about: Asks when growers can again obtain inspected seed oysters from Sendai Bay.
subfiles.summary: The association describes the prewar trade and its preference for direct dealings with Sendai Bay growers. It asks about the 1945 seed catch, available quantities, timing and the appropriate negotiating authority.

subfiles.title: Reply to Savage on Japanese seed-oyster trade
subfiles.about: Explains that direct trade with Japanese seed-oyster suppliers cannot yet resume.
subfiles.summary: Byrnes says occupation priorities prevent near-term direct dealings. The Department lacks figures for the 1945 catch but will forward them when available; any exportable seed might later be offered through Allied authorities.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Foreign Economic Administration reports
subfiles.about: Transmits copies of reports, including one on Japanese light metals.
subfiles.summary: A short distribution note accompanies the reports.

subfiles.title: Postwar Control of the Japanese Light Metals Industry
subfiles.about: Recommends controls over Japanese aluminum and magnesium production, processing, stocks and imports.
subfiles.summary: The report argues that Japan’s light metals industry was built for war and exceeded plausible civilian needs. It recommends removing or destroying metal-producing plants, limiting fabrication equipment, inventorying existing stocks and controlling imports. Its appendices list Japanese plants and capacities, production and trade figures, raw-material sources, manufacturing processes and comparative U.S. employment data.

subfiles.title: Administration of Production Programs in Japan
subfiles.doc_type: Foreign Economic Administration guide; continues after page 74
subfiles.about: Begins a guide for military-government control of Japanese industrial production.
subfiles.summary: A cover warning says the recommendations preceded Japan’s surrender and require review against current policy. The opening pages set out the guide’s scope and recommend priorities, material allocations and credit for essential production. They propose initially retaining Japanese control rules and agencies, then redirecting resources toward civilian needs and reshaping the wartime economy.
